claim: The Recognition scene does not say the speaker is leaving, so it fits the entering card shitsurei-shimasu-entering just as well and the learner cannot tell 'Good-bye.' from 'Excuse me.'
evidence: Recognition front: 'しつれいします / said on formal occasions'. Other card shitsurei-shimasu-entering, Recognition front: 'しつれいします / said when entering another person's room', answer 'Excuse me.' Entering a boss's office is also a formal occasion; the word 'leaving' appears only on the back hint ('the formal way out: leaving a boss's office or a meeting').
fix: Make the scene name the leaving, e.g. 'said when leaving, on formal occasions'.
verdictReason: Checked both fronts: the entering card's own hint names 'someone's office, a meeting room or an interview', all formal occasions, so 'said on formal occasions' covers both targets and separates nothing on Recognition. The scene is the book's parenthetical (panel 7), but the book prints 'Good-bye.' beside it and the front does not. The collision rule requires a scene that picks one answer, and the rules accept a small leak for a shared target; panel 7's picture (bowing with a briefcase at the lift) is a leaving scene, so adding 'when leaving' stays faithful.

claim: The scene on the Recognition front restates the answer, so the face tests nothing.
evidence: Recognition front: 'いただきます / about to start eating'; back answer: '(Said before eating a meal)'. The Production front repeats it too: '(Said before eating a meal) / about to start eating'. There is only one いただきます card, and gochisousama-deshita ('(Said after eating a meal)') ships with no scene and works.
fix: Drop the scene, as on gochisousama-deshita, since no other card shares this target.
verdictReason: The scene does echo the answer, but it is a required collision cue, not a free leak: いただきます is carded three times in this collection (chapter-10 itadakimasu-accept 'Yes, thank you.', scene 'accepting something you have just been offered'; chapter-17 itadakimasu-2 'Let's eat'), so the target rule demands a scene on this card. Its English IS the situation ('(Said before eating a meal)', the book's own gloss), so any scene that separates it from the offer-accepting use must paraphrase it; card-authoring-rules names that leak as the accepted price of an answerable card. The proposed fix (drop the scene) would un-cue a target collision preflight currently reports clean. Learner saw an empty ledger, so 'only one card' was true from its seat but not for the shuffled deck.

claim: The note's last clause ('not a direct answer to a yes/no question') can be read as saying いいえ never answers a yes/no question, and nothing tells a first-unit learner that the word's plain meaning is 'no', which the book teaches in Lesson 1.
evidence: Note: 'A polite way to deflect thanks or a compliment, roughly 'not at all' or 'don't mention it' — not a direct answer to a yes/no question.' Book, Lesson 1: 'はい is virtually the same as "yes," and いいえ is virtually the same as "no."'
fix: Reword the clause to say that in this use it deflects thanks rather than answering a question, and that the same word is the plain 'no' in answer to a yes/no question. Keep the contrast: chapter-1's iie ('No', scene 'answering a yes-or-no question') shares the target and this clause is its relationship note.
verdictReason: Both roles read the same clause the same way, independently. Checked Lesson 1 (chapters/14.xhtml): 'いいえ is virtually the same as "no"', and chapter-1 carries iie 'No' with scene 'answering a yes-or-no question'. The clause is this card's relationship note for that target collision, so it is doing a required job and is not false, but with an empty ledger it is the only thing the learner has on the word and reads as a property of the word. Reword it to say this USE is not a yes/no answer and that the plain meaning is 'no' (stating the meaning is not a forward card reference). Keep the clause's contrast, since the chapter-1 collision still needs it.

claim: The hint calls this the 'full-length form', implying a shorter form, but neither the hint nor the note says what that shorter form is.
evidence: Production front: 'Thank you. / the polite full-length form, for a stranger or a superior'. Note: 'The standard, all-purpose polite 'thank you' — safe in almost any situation, from shops to business settings.'
fix: Name the short form in the note (ありがとう, arigatō, for friends), or drop 'full-length' from the hint.
verdictReason: Verified: the hint says 'full-length' and neither hint nor note names the short form. The hint is a mandated English-collision cue ('Thank you.' is also chapter-3 doumo-arigatou, hint 'warm but casual'; cf. chapter-26 arigatou-thanks 'Thanks. (casual)'), so the contrast must stay; the fixer should add the short form to the note (as the gochisousama-deshita note does for ごちそうさま) rather than drop 'full-length' from the hint. Naming ありがとう as the casual short form is a gloss, not a forward card reference.

claim: The note says when to use the phrase but not what おさきに adds to しつれいします, which the learner already knows from two other cards.
evidence: Note: 'Said by the person leaving work before their colleagues; the colleagues who remain reply with おつかれさまでした (otsukaresama deshita) to the one leaving.' The parts おさき and に are never glossed, while chotto-matte-kudasai and mou-ichido-onegaishimasu break their phrases into parts.
fix: Add a short breakdown: おさきに (osaki ni, 'ahead of you') + しつれいします, roughly 'excuse me for going first'.
verdictReason: True as stated: おさきに is glossed nowhere on the card, and the book (panel 8) does not gloss it either, so the card is faithful and answerable. Whether to add a breakdown is an editorial choice that pulls against the merged chotto-matte-kudasai finding, which asks the two request-phrase notes to stop breaking phrases into untaught parts. What settles it: the owner picking one convention for this set-phrase unit (gloss the pieces in plain words, or teach each phrase whole). A one-line gloss 'おさきに (osaki ni, ahead of you)' needs no grammar and fits either way.

claim: Both notes explain the phrase with the て-form of まつ and a softness ranking of おねがいします over ください, which no card has taught, a first-unit learner cannot unpack, and the book does not say at this point.
evidence: Note: 'まって is the て-form of まつ (matsu, 'to wait') plus ください (kudasai). ください attaches directly onto a verb's て-form for a fairly direct ask'. The mou-ichido-onegaishimasu note repeats 'attaches directly to a verb's て-form'. The ledger is empty. Book panel 14 gives only 'ちょっと　まってください。 Wait just a moment, please.' as a whole phrase. Card note: 'まって is the て-form of まつ (matsu, 'to wait') plus ください (kudasai). ください attaches directly onto a verb's て-form for a fairly direct ask; contrast もういちどおねがいします ..., which uses the standalone, slightly softer おねがいします instead.' The mou-ichido-onegaishimasu note repeats the 'somewhat softer' comparison.
fix: Trim both notes to what each phrase means and when it is said, or say it in plain words (まって is the form of まつ that ください attaches to) without the grammar label; leave the て-form explanation to the lesson that teaches it.
verdictReason: Same problem from both seats. Ledger is empty (0 cards taught), so 'て-form' is untaught; panel 14 gives the phrase whole with no breakdown, and nothing in the chapter ranks おねがいします against ください for softness. The grammar in the note is correct Japanese, so this is a reach beyond what the learner can use, not an error: polish. The fix should cover both notes (chotto-matte-kudasai and mou-ichido-onegaishimasu repeat each other).

claim: The note spells the romaji 'gochisousama' while the card's Says line spells it 'gochisōsama', and preflight's inline romaji check does not list this instance.
evidence: Says: 'gochisōsama (deshita).' Note: 'ごちそうさまでした (gochisousama deshita) is the fuller, formal version, while ごちそうさま (gochisousama) alone is the casual short form.' The itadakimasu note has the same spelling: 'ごちそうさま（でした） (gochisousama (deshita))'.
fix: Use 'gochisōsama' in both notes to match the card.
verdictReason: Verified on the rendered back: Says 'gochisōsama (deshita).' vs note '(gochisousama deshita)' and '(gochisousama)', and the itadakimasu note repeats it. Preflight's inline-romaji check misses it because it keys quoted text against a card's exact target and ごちそうさま / ごちそうさまでした do not match ごちそうさま（でした）; the same gap hides 'otsukaresama deshita' in the otsukaresama-deshita note. The pinned romaji style (macrons, never 'ou') applies to anything hand-written, so this is a real but cosmetic mismatch. Note the whole unit's notes use 'ou' spellings (preflight lists three more), so a fixer should sweep the unit's notes once rather than one card.

claim: The note calls こんにちは a neutral greeting, but the book describes it as rather informal.
evidence: Book panel 2: 'Hello./Good afternoon. (A rather informal greeting used from about 10:00 A.M. until sundown.)' Card note: 'A neutral daytime greeting used from about 10:00 A.M. until sundown'.
fix: Replace 'neutral' with the book's 'rather informal' in the note.
verdictReason: Read panel 2 of the page image: '(A rather informal greeting used from about 10:00 A.M. until sundown.)' The note keeps the hours but swaps the book's register label for 'neutral', which is the one thing the book says about the word beyond its hours. Straight mismatch, one-word fix.

claim: The hint and note restrict さようなら to final, fairly formal partings, which the book's own panel contradicts and which blurs the book's contrast with the formal しつれいします.
evidence: Book panel 5: 'さようなら。 Good-bye.' illustrated by a teacher waving to two schoolchildren with school bags (people who meet daily); panel 7 gives the formal good-bye as 'しつれいします。 Good-bye. (Said on formal occasions.)'. Card hint (on the Production front): 'sounds final, so not for friends, family or colleagues you will see again soon'; note: 'A fairly formal, somewhat final-sounding goodbye'. The ja-mata note repeats it: 'for a more formal parting use さようなら (sayounara) or しつれいします'.
fix: Drop 'fairly formal' and the 'not for ... you will see again soon' restriction from the hint and note (and the ja-mata note), keeping the book's plain 'Good-bye' with a scene that fits its picture.
verdictReason: Read panels 5 and 7: さようなら is glossed only 'Good-bye.' with a teacher waving to two schoolchildren, people who meet daily, and the book reserves 'formal occasions' for しつれいします. The hint's 'not for ... colleagues you will see again soon' and the note's 'fairly formal' both go beyond the book and the picture contradicts the first; the ja-mata note repeats the framing. Constraint for the fixer: 'Good-bye.' is shared by four cards (shitsurei-shimasu-leaving, osaki-ni-shitsurei-shimasu, otsukaresama-deshita), so sayounara must keep a cue; replace the hint with one that fits the picture (e.g. the everyday good-bye, as a teacher to pupils), do not drop it.

claim: The note points the learner at 'the source', which a learner reviewing in Anki does not have.
evidence: Note: 'Suffix — attaches after a person's name; cannot be used after one's own name (written 〜さん (san) in the source)'.
fix: Drop the 'in the source' aside, or say what the 〜 means (something goes in front) without citing the book.

'The source' is the book, which a learner reviewing in Anki does not have; the useful content (the 〜 marks where the name goes) can be said without citing it. Same generated phrasing recurs on chapter-3 (ji, han, fun) and chapter-4 (en) suffix cards, so this is a pattern, not a one-off.

claim: The English defines どちら by reference to どこ, a word no earlier card and no card in this chapter teaches.

The comparison is the chapter's, not the deck's: the book does it that way.

claim: The card needs を, which the learner has never seen, and the note names it without saying what it does; the English 'Please (I'd like to see Tanaka-san)' also reads oddly as a prompt.

fix: Use the English 'I'd like to see Tanaka-san, please.' with a reception-desk hint, and add one clause saying を marks the person you are asking for.

The same frame ships in the extras as w2-harris-o-onegaishimasu with the natural 'I'd like to see Harris-san, please.' and a note explaining を; this card's note names を without saying what it marks, and no card in chapter 1 teaches を on its own (the book lists only 〜を おねがいします). Polish: the card is answerable and faithful, just awkward and under-explained next to its sibling.

claim: The romaji splits ドイツじん as 'doitsu jin', while the deck's own ドイツじん card spells it 'doitsujin'.

The style guide's word-segmentation rule ('split into WORDS, not syllables') agrees, and preflight's word-segmentation lint only detects mase/masu/deshi/n fragments, so it did not catch this.

claim: The target introduces someone else with こちらは but leaves さん off their name, which contradicts what every other card in this chapter teaches about naming another person.
evidence: Answer: 'こちらはイギリスのライアンです' ('This is Ryan from England'). Compare w2-kochira-hoffman note: 'さん (san) stays on because you are naming somebody else', and san-suffix-ch14: 'cannot be used after one's own name'. ks3-tanaka-nozomi, fib-c1-this-is-brown and w2-kochira-harris all keep さん after こちらは. | Reader: Book: こちら 'this one (polite for "this person")'; KS3 'こちらは のぞみデパートの たなかさんです'; Exercise V 'こちらは ベルリンモーターズの ホフマンさんです'; NOTES 'さん ... cannot be used after one's own name'. Card: 'こちらはイギリスのライアンです' / 'This is Ryan from England'.
fix: Either add さん (こちらはイギリスのライアンさんです) or add a note explaining when さん is dropped when introducing someone; also gloss イギリス as 'the United Kingdom' to match the igirisu card.
verdictReason: Target こちらはイギリスのライアンです introduces a third person with こちらは and a bare name. Book: こちら 'this one (polite for this person)'; KS3, Exercise V and Speaking Practice 2 all print こちらは…さんです; NOTES 1 limits bare names to one's own. Every other こちらは card in both units keeps さん (ks3-tanaka-nozomi, fib-c1-this-is-brown, w2-kochira-harris, w2-kochira-hoffman, w2-sp2-sasaki-intro), and w2-kochira-hoffman's note states the rule outright, so this card contradicts the chapter's teaching with no note. (Dropping さん for a member of your own group is real Japanese, but nothing at this level teaches it.) Both roles found it independently; merged. The card came in from the owner's Nihongo 101 absorption (addition nihongo-102-2026-08), so the owner may want to say which fix.

claim: The note claims a name without さん 'can only mean' yourself, but another card in this unit uses a bare name for someone else.

Settled by the irl-l1-28 fix: if さん is added there the deck's examples all agree with the note and nothing needs changing; if irl-l1-28 instead keeps the bare name with an in-group note, soften this to 'normally means'.

claim: The note says every other の in the lesson joins a company to a person, which the learner can see is false from other cards in this unit.

fix: Say instead that here の marks possession, as opposed to the company-and-person の of the introductions.

In the same unit ラジャさんのおくに (w2-raja-no-okuni-q), わたしのくに (w2-watashi-no-kuni-nihon) and イギリスのライアン (irl-l1-28) all use の for plain possession or origin. claim: The note splits the two meanings by intonation and gives 'Is that so?' to rising intonation, but the book gives both meanings to one expression that is spoken with falling intonation.

Card note: "Falling intonation = 'I see' (acknowledging what you heard); rising intonation = 'Is that so? / Really?' (a genuine question)." The note also says そうです confirms "your own statement", which is not what そうです does in Lesson 1. Learner: Note: 'rather than confirming your own statement like そうです (sou desu) does'. The card note gives 'Is that so? / Really?' to rising intonation as 'a genuine question', which the book does not say. The そうです half is wrong too: chapter-1/sou-desu's own note reads 'Confirms or affirms a statement outright (that's right)' and chapter-1-extras/hai-sou-desu is a reply to a question, so そうです confirms what the other person said, not 'your own statement'. claim: The English renders からです as 'at', so the card loses から, which the book always glosses as 'from'.

Book KS3 glosses the same shape 'The meeting is tomorrow, from 4:00.', the drill it comes from (EXERCISES V) answers with からです, and the deck's own cards agree: kaigi-ashita-kuji-a 'It's from 9:00 tomorrow.', sumisu-purezen-a 'It's from 3:00 P.M. today.', and rasuto-oodaa-niji-desu's note says plain です pins a moment while からです means it starts then. claim: The note says いつ asks which day, but the book's model answer to this exact question gives a day and an hour.

claim: The Recognition front's hint contains the answer word, so the card is read rather than recalled.

The scene itself is mandatory: まで collides with chapter-19/made 'To, as far as (particle)' (scene 'marking how far along a route you are travelling'), so the fix is to reword, not drop. claim: The Recognition front's hint points straight at the meaning it asks for.

claim: The Recognition front's hint is a paraphrase of the answer.

claim: The Production English is the gloss of うけつけ from Lesson 1, so I answer うけつけ and am marked wrong.

The book glosses フロント as 'reception desk', so keep the gloss and add hints: 'at a hotel' on furonto (its own back note already says so) and 'an office or building, not a hotel' on uketsuke.

claim: The target writes the hour as the digit ７, which I read as なな, hiding the irregular しち reading the card is supposed to drill.

Reading ７じ as しちじ is the skill the book trains from here; it is not hidden, it is tested.

claim: 'Reception desk' again cues うけつけ from Lesson 1 rather than フロント.

No うけつけ sentence collides, so polish is right, but a hint on the word card does not reach this sentence; say 'the hotel front desk' in the English here and in furonto-a's scene ('answering the reception desk's opening hours').

claim: さんぷん takes ぷん with no change to the number, and nothing tells me why; the base unit's minute cards never used 3 or 4.
evidence: Recognition front: 'さんぷん'. Back: 'Answer: Three minutes | Says: sanpun', no note. The はっぷん, ろっぷん, いっぷん cards each get a note explaining their change.

claim: よんぷん takes ぷん with no explanation, unlike the other irregular minute cards.

claim: The note describes the card's place in a set of cards, which means nothing when the cards come shuffled.
evidence: Note: 'Member 1 of a です / じゃありません / ですか set built on one time, so the change is in the ending and nothing else.' The siblings ima-kuji-ja-arimasen and ima-kuji-desu-ka also say 'Member 2' and 'Member 3 of the set'.

verdictReason: Note reads in full: 'Member 1 of a です / じゃありません / ですか set built on one time, so the change is in the ending and nothing else.' It describes where the card sits in an authoring set, which a shuffled learner never sees, and says nothing about the sentence; the rules say a self-evident sentence should carry no note rather than one that adds nothing. The siblings' notes (ima-kuji-ja-arimasen 'Member 2 of the set begun by…', ima-kuji-desu-ka 'Member 3 of the set:') open with real content and can simply lose the 'Member N' clause.

claim: The note leads with a book section label I do not have.

Drop the label, keep the rule. The same label problem sits on toukyou-ima-gogo-yoji-han ('GRAMMAR 1: naming another place makes it the topic…'), which neither role filed; the fixer should sweep it in the same edit.

claim: The note cites a book section as its authority, which I cannot open.

claim: やすみ was taught as 'a pause during the day', and here it means a day off, so the card contradicts the word card's hint.
evidence: Production front: 'Time | When is your day off?'. Base card やすみ: 'Break, time off | a pause during the day'. yasumi-ashita-a: 'It's tomorrow. | answering when the day off is'.

claim: GRAMMAR 3 contrasts かかります (a time felt as long) with "period です" (a time not felt as long); the card gives only the first half and no card in either unit teaches the second.

verdictReason: Merged with the Learner's note-unverifiable finding on the same note. The Learner's claim that the book does not make this statement is wrong: GRAMMAR 3 says かかります "is used when the speaker considers the time to be long", and the book's own example is 40 minutes, so the 15/30-minute extras do not contradict it and the clause must not be dropped. What is true in both findings is that the note gives half of the book's contrast: GRAMMAR 3 continues "When the speaker does not feel the time to be long, period です is used", and a grep of both units for ぷんです/じかんです/かんです/ねんです finds no card or note carrying that half. claim: GRAMMAR 3 and 4 both teach that a length of time goes straight before かかります or います with no particle after it, and no card back states this.

Regular 1."; imasu-stay note "With a length of time it means you stay somewhere for that long."; gr4-london-3nen-imashita note "ぐらい after the period makes it approximate". claim: The English asks me to 'pay by card', and the only way I was taught to pay by card is カードで, so I don't get to つかって from this front.

claim: The English says 'my phone', and an earlier note told me スマホ means a smartphone specifically while けいたい is the general mobile phone, so I answer with けいたい.

claim: Same problem as charge-my-phone: 'my phone' makes me say けいたい, and the answer is スマホ.

verdictReason: おしごとはですか is not a sentence; what is elided is なんですか. The deck's own earlier note on chapter-25-extras りょうりは? says it 'leaves the rest of the question unsaid', so this note also disagrees with the deck.

claim: An authored card rests on もう with a negative meaning "no longer", a use the book has not taught; the deck taught もう only as "already" (Lesson 23).

The book never teaches 'no longer' (grep of every chapter), so swapping to a plain negative is an owner taste call, not a rule breach.
